t: The Phoenicians were the Iron Age heirs of the Canaanite towns of the Lebanese coast: not one nation but rival city-states such as Tyre, Sidon, Byblos and Arwad, each with its own king.
Their merchants sold cedar, purple cloth, ivory and metalwork across the Near East, and from the 9th century BCE founded settlements from Cyprus to Spain, among them Carthage.
Their alphabet of 22 letters, taken up by the Greeks and the Aramaeans, is the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.
dyk: Herodotus tells how Phoenician sailors sent by the pharaoh Necho II sailed round Africa in three years. He doubted their report that the sun had been on their right, the very detail that leads many scholars to take the voyage seriously.
ev: The Late Bronze Age kingdoms collapse; the cities of the Lebanese coast emerge as independent kingdoms
The sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos is inscribed in the Phoenician alphabet
Hiram I makes Tyre the leading city; by the biblical account he sends cedar for Solomon’s temple
Tyrians traditionally found Carthage, as settlements spread to Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain
Esarhaddon of Assyria captures rebellious Sidon and deports its people
Tyre withstands a thirteen-year siege by Nebuchadnezzar II
The cities pass under Persian rule; their ships form the core of the Persian navy
Alexander the Great takes Tyre after a siege of about seven months

f.homeland: The coast of the northern Levant, chiefly present-day Lebanon with neighbouring parts of Syria and northern Israel; settlements on Cyprus, Malta, Sicily and Sardinia, in North Africa and in southern Spain
f.period: c. 1200–332 BCE, from the collapse of the Late Bronze Age kingdoms to Alexander the Great’s capture of Tyre; in the west, Punic Carthage carried the culture on until 146 BCE
f.known: The alphabet; Tyrian purple and the cedar trade; seafaring and colonies such as Carthage and Gadir (Cádiz); carved ivories, decorated metal bowls and glass
f.sources: Excavations at Byblos, Sidon, Tyre, Sarepta, Kition, Motya and Carthage; inscriptions such as those of Ahiram, Tabnit and Eshmunazar II; the Hebrew Bible, Assyrian royal annals, the Story of Wenamun, Homer, Herodotus and Josephus
